Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\widetilde{\deg}_+(f) \le \deg(f)\)
    An exact representation is a one-sided approximation with room to spare: $p = 0$ on $f^{-1}(0)$ satisfies $|p| \le 1/3$, and $p = 1$ on $f^{-1}(1)$ satisfies $p \ge 2/3$. The one-sided constraints are imposed on $\mathrm{Dom}(f)$ only, so nothing is asked of $p$ off the promise.

Worth contrasting with $\widetilde{\deg} \le \deg$, which fails on \(\mathrm{SEARCH}^{\le 1}_n\): the two-sided measure is the one that carries an off-promise boundedness requirement, and that requirement is the whole difference.

see also: \(\widetilde{\deg}_{+}(f)\), \(\deg(f)\), \(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{SEARCH}^{\le 1}_n\) data/relations/13-definitional.yaml

up.note: An $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial satisfies the one-sided constraints -- a pointwise implication at each $x \in \mathrm{Dom}(f)$, so a containment of feasible sets in any setting. (One-sided approximate degree is in fact most used for partial functions, where it is the natural measure for one-sided error.)

lo.note: The one-sided relaxation buys nothing on the AND side: a polynomial bounded on all of $\{0,1\}^n \setminus \{1^n\}$ and large at $1^n$ still needs degree $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ by the Markov-brothers argument.

  • \(\widetilde{\deg}_+(\mathrm{AND}_n) = \widetilde{\deg}(\mathrm{AND}_n) = \Theta(\sqrt n)\)
    witness: \(\mathrm{AND}_n\) NS94 Paturi92
    The one-sided relaxation buys nothing on the AND side: a polynomial bounded on all of $\{0,1\}^n \setminus \{1^n\}$ and large at $1^n$ still needs degree $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ by the Markov-brothers argument.
  • \(\widetilde{\deg}_+(\mathrm{PARITY}_n) = \widetilde{\deg}(\mathrm{PARITY}_n) = n\)
    witness: \(\oplus_n\) MinskyPapert69 NS94
    Squeezed with no room at all: $\mathrm{sdeg}(\oplus_n) = n \le \widetilde{\deg}_+(\oplus_n) \le \widetilde{\deg}(\oplus_n) = n$. So on parity one-sidedness buys literally nothing, not even a constant.
see also: \(\widetilde{\deg}_{+}(f)\), \(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{sdeg}(f)\), \(\deg(f)\) data/relations/10-new-measures.yaml

facts: $\mathrm{sdeg}(f) \le \widetilde{\deg}_+(f) \le \widetilde{\deg}(f) \le \deg(f)$: an approximating polynomial is one-sided, and a one-sided one shifted by $1/2$ sign-represents $f$.

Both inequalities can be maximally loose, in opposite directions. $\widetilde{\deg}_+(\mathrm{OR}_n) = 1$ (take $p = \sum_i x_i$) while $\widetilde{\deg}(\mathrm{OR}_n) = \Theta(\sqrt n)$; $\mathrm{sdeg}(\mathrm{AND}_n) = 1$ while $\widetilde{\deg}_+(\mathrm{AND}_n) = \Theta(\sqrt n)$.

So $\widetilde{\deg}_+$ is not symmetric under negation: $\widetilde{\deg}_+(\mathrm{OR}_n) = 1$ but $\widetilde{\deg}_+(\mathrm{AND}_n) = \Theta(\sqrt n)$, and $\mathrm{AND}_n = \overline{\mathrm{OR}_n(\bar x)}$.
$\max\{\widetilde{\deg}_+(f), \widetilde{\deg}_+(\bar f)\}$ is not known to be $\Theta(\widetilde{\deg}(f))$; recovering a two-sided approximation from two one-sided ones loses.
Used to prove $\widetilde{\deg}(\mathrm{AC}^0) = \Omega(n^{1-\delta})$ by composing one-sided dual witnesses [Sherstov14onesided, BunThaler17].
self.name: One-sided approximate degree
self.short: Approximate degree when the polynomial only has to be *large* on 1-inputs, not close to 1.
